title: Book review: The Catchment as an Archive
intro: A new book argues that landscapes keep records — and that reading them is a skill we are quietly losing.

add_image.image_alt: A book open on a desk beside field notes
add_image.image_caption: The Catchment as an Archive, read beside a season of notebooks.
add_image.content_to_show_on_side_of_the_image_whe: The book is at its best when it stays close to the ground: a chapter on bank erosion, another on seed banks, a third on the strata of a single pasture. The argument is that these are not metaphors for memory but memory itself, written in material that can be read if you know the grammar.

add_table.heading: At a glance
content_of_rows_separated_by_comma: Title, The Catchment as an Archive
Best for, Field scientists and historians of landscape

add_quote.text: The strongest chapters are the least theoretical: a single core, read slowly, with the patience the author asks of everyone else.

add_focus_list.heading: Verdict
items_of_the_focus_list: Excellent on method and close observation.
Thin on the policy implications it gestures at.
Worth the time for anyone who works in a catchment.

add_special_note.heading: Read this if
add_special_note.text: You have ever stood in a river and wondered how much of what you are seeing is recent. The book gives you the vocabulary, not a formula.
